title: Elementary Graph Theory
intro: Graphs, trees, Euler and Hamilton, planarity and spanning trees at a glance.

sec.s: Graph theory studies relationships between objects.

b.x: Graph theory studies relationships between objects. A graph is written G = (V, E), where V is the set of vertices (nodes) and E is the set of edges connecting them. Examples include social networks, road networks, computer networks, and hyperlinks.
Unless stated otherwise, these notes focus on finite undirected graphs without loops or parallel edges, then introduce special graph types.

b.x: Handshaking Lemma
Sum of degrees of all vertices = 2|E|.
Each edge contributes 1 to the degree of each endpoint, so it contributes 2 to the total degree.
Corollary: Every finite undirected graph has an even number of odd-degree vertices.

Walk
A sequence of vertices where consecutive vertices are connected by edges; vertices and edges may repeat.
Trail
A walk with no repeated edges.
Path
A walk with no repeated vertices. Its length is its number of edges.
Closed walk
A walk that begins and ends at the same vertex.
Circuit
Often means a closed trail; terminology varies slightly by textbook.
Cycle
A closed path with no repeated vertices other than the starting/ending vertex. In a simple graph, a cycle normally has at least three edges.
Connected graph
An undirected graph with a path between every pair of distinct vertices.
Disconnected graph
A graph in which some pair of vertices has no path between them.
Connected component
A maximal connected part of a graph.
Distance d(u,v)
Length of a shortest path between u and v.
Diameter
The largest distance between any pair of vertices in a connected graph.
Cut-vertex
A vertex whose removal increases the number of connected components.
Bridge/cut-edge
An edge whose removal increases the number of connected components.

b.x: Basic results

x: A graph is connected exactly when it has one connected component.
Every connected graph with n vertices has at least n - 1 edges.
A connected graph with n vertices and n - 1 edges is a tree.
Removing an edge from a cycle does not disconnect a connected graph.

b.x: H = (V_H, E_H) is a subgraph of G = (V,E) if V_H is a subset of V and E_H is a subset of E, with each selected edge having both endpoints in V_H.

x: Proper subgraph
Not equal to the original graph.
Spanning subgraph
Contains every vertex of the original graph.
Induced subgraph on S
Contains the vertices in S and every original edge whose endpoints are both in S.
If G has vertices A, B, C, D and edges AB, BC, CD, AC, the induced subgraph on {A,B,C} has edges AB, BC, and AC.

sec.s: A weighted graph assigns a number to each edge or arc.

b.x: A weighted graph assigns a number to each edge or arc. Weights may represent distance, cost, time, capacity, or risk. The weight of a path is normally the sum of its edge weights.
A shortest-path problem seeks a path of minimum total weight. A minimum spanning tree seeks a spanning tree with minimum total edge weight. Ordinary road-distance weights are usually non-negative.

x: Euler trail
A trail using every edge exactly once; vertices may repeat.
Euler circuit
An Euler trail that starts and ends at the same vertex.
Eulerian graph
A connected graph with at least one edge that has an Euler circuit.

b.x: Euler's theorem for undirected graphs

x: A connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree.
It has an open Euler trail but no Euler circuit if and only if exactly two vertices have odd degree.
If more than two vertices have odd degree, it has neither.

b.x: For these tests, isolated vertices may be disregarded, but all vertices incident with edges must be in one connected component.

x: A triangle has degree 2 at each vertex, so it has an Euler circuit. A simple path has two odd-degree endpoints and has an Euler trail from one endpoint to the other.

b.x: Applications: Route planning when every edge or road must be traversed, such as inspection and street-sweeping routes. The Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem is a classic origin of graph theory.

sec.s: A graph can be Eulerian, Hamiltonian, both, or neither.

x: Hamiltonian path
A path visiting every vertex exactly once.
Hamiltonian cycle
A cycle visiting every vertex exactly once and returning to the start.
Hamiltonian graph
A graph containing a Hamiltonian cycle.

b.x: Eulerian versus Hamiltonian

x: Eulerian focuses on using every edge exactly once.
Hamiltonian focuses on visiting every vertex exactly once.

b.x: A graph can be Eulerian, Hamiltonian, both, or neither.
Sufficient conditions

x: Dirac's theorem
A simple graph with n ≥ 3 vertices is Hamiltonian if every vertex has degree at least n/2.
Ore's theorem
A simple graph with n ≥ 3 vertices is Hamiltonian if every pair of non-adjacent vertices u and v satisfies deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n.

b.x: These are sufficient, not necessary, conditions. A graph may be Hamiltonian without satisfying them. There is no simple degree-only test that decides Hamiltonicity for all graphs.

x: Tree
A connected undirected graph with no cycles.
Forest
An acyclic undirected graph; each connected component is a tree.
Rooted tree
A tree with one selected vertex called the root.
Parent/child
Immediate relationships in a rooted tree.
Siblings
Vertices with the same parent.
Ancestor/descendant
Vertices above/below one another in the rooted structure.
Leaf
In an unrooted tree, a vertex of degree 1; in a rooted tree, commonly a vertex with no children.
Internal vertex
A non-leaf vertex.

b.x: Properties of a tree T with n vertices

x: It has exactly n - 1 edges.
There is exactly one simple path between every pair of vertices.
Removing any edge disconnects it.
Adding an edge between existing vertices creates exactly one cycle.
Every tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves.
Every tree is bipartite.
It is minimally connected: removing any edge destroys connectivity.
It is maximally acyclic: adding an edge creates a cycle.

b.x: Equivalent characterisations for a finite undirected graph

x: It is a tree.
It is connected and has n - 1 edges.
It is acyclic and has n - 1 edges.
There is exactly one simple path between every pair of vertices.
It is connected and every edge is a bridge.
It is acyclic, and adding any edge between existing vertices creates a cycle.

b.x: Proof idea for n - 1 edges: A tree with one vertex has zero edges. Every larger tree has a leaf. Removing a leaf and its edge leaves a smaller tree. Repeating until one vertex remains shows that each of the other n - 1 vertices contributes one edge.

x: Binary tree
A rooted tree where each vertex has at most two children.
Full binary tree
Every internal vertex has exactly two children. For a full binary tree, if I is the number of internal vertices and L is the number of leaves, then L = I + 1 and total vertices n = 2I + 1.

sec.s: A spanning tree of a connected graph is a subgraph that contains every vertex and is connected and acyclic.

b.x: A spanning tree of a connected graph is a subgraph that contains every vertex and is connected and acyclic. Every spanning tree on n vertices has n - 1 edges. A connected graph may have multiple spanning trees; a tree's only spanning tree is itself.
Finding a spanning tree

x: Start with a connected graph.
Find a cycle and remove one edge from that cycle.
Repeat until no cycles remain.

b.x: Connectivity is preserved and the result is a spanning tree.
Minimum spanning tree (MST): A spanning tree of a connected weighted undirected graph with the minimum possible sum of edge weights.
Kruskal's algorithm

x: Sort edges by increasing weight.
Consider edges from smallest to largest.
Add an edge only if it does not create a cycle.
Stop after selecting n - 1 edges.

b.x: Prim's algorithm

x: Start from any vertex.
Repeatedly select a minimum-weight edge joining the current tree to a vertex outside it.
Stop when all vertices are included.

b.x: If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique. If weights repeat, multiple MSTs may exist.

sec.s: Planar graph: A graph that can be drawn in the plane so edges meet only at shared endpoints.

b.x: Planar graph: A graph that can be drawn in the plane so edges meet only at shared endpoints. A crossing-free drawing is a plane embedding. A graph may have a crossing in one drawing but still be planar if another crossing-free drawing exists.
Faces: Regions formed by a plane embedding, including the unbounded outside region.

For c connected components, the formula is V - E + F = 1 + c.

b.x: Important non-planar graphs

x: K5
Complete graph on five vertices, with 10 edges. Since 10 > 3(5) - 6 = 9, it is non-planar.
Complete bipartite graph with two sets of three vertices. It has V = 6 and E = 9, and no triangles. The triangle-free bound gives E ≤ 2(6) - 4 = 8, so it is non-planar.

b.x: Kuratowski's theorem (basic statement): A finite graph is planar if and only if it contains no subgraph that is a subdivision of K5 or K3,3. Subdivision means replacing edges by paths with new vertices inserted along them.
Applications include map drawing, circuit layouts, and region-related problems.

sec.s: A graph is bipartite if its vertices can be divided into two disjoint sets A and B so every edge joins a…

b.x: A graph is bipartite if its vertices can be divided into two disjoint sets A and B so every edge joins a vertex in A to a vertex in B; no edge joins two vertices in the same part.
Complete bipartite graph K(m,n): Every vertex in one part is connected to every vertex in the other part. It has mn edges.
A graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle.
Every tree is bipartite. K3,3 is bipartite and non-planar. K2,3 has 2 x 3 = 6 edges.
